To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we have developed a methodology to measure the effective evolutionary games played by cancer cell populations, and that this methodology can reveal how the type of game can change in the presence of cancer associated fibroblast and drug treatment.
the growth rate of cancer cell co cultures is quantitatively described by an evolutionary game and that drug treatment alters this game from 'leader' to 'deadlock'.
the growth rates of drug sensitive and resistant cancer cells co cultured together can be quantitatively described by an evolutionary game.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a novel methodology to measure the fitness landscape of cancer cell populations and the effects of cancer therapy and the tumor microenvironment on that landscape.
understanding the role of non cell autonomous interactions in shaping the evolutionary dynamics of cancer.
the evolution of resistance in cancer.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
this work provides a new method to measure the evolutionary games played in a population of cancer cells, and that these games are altered by targeted therapy and cancer-associated fibroblasts.
the game played in vitro is not Leader, but Deadlock, and that this is due to the presence of fibroblasts.
the game theory model of the growth rate data is a good fit to the data.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
alectinib and fibroblasts switch the evolutionary games of non small cell Lung Cancer cells in vitro.
alectinib and fibroblasts switch the evolutionary games being played by the non small cell lung cancers we studied.

we have shown that evolutionary game theory can be applied to the in vitro measurement of cancer cell populations and that this application can be used to study how the game played by a cancer cell population changes in response to drug treatment and to fibroblast co culture.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can treat not just the player, but the game.
cancer is not a game of survival of the fittest, but rather a game of survival and proliferation of the fittest.
the game played by a population can change in response to environmental changes, and that we can treat the game as well as the player.
